What

What Emergency Tree Service Actually Covers

Storm response isn't just cutting a tree off a roof. Here's what a full Roubic emergency response looks like from the first call to the insurance handoff.

Storm Damage & Emergency Tree Care covers immediate-response removal and cleanup of fallen, leaning, split, or partially-failed trees. Scope includes tree-on-structure extraction (tree on house, garage, vehicle, fence, pool), removal of branches on or near power lines (coordinated with FirstEnergy / Illuminating Company), site-safety control during the response, insurance-claim documentation, and post-storm property-wide debris cleanup. We answer the phone 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, with response times measured in hours rather than days.

Why

Why Storm Response Time Matters

When a tree fails on or near a structure, every hour of delay compounds the damage. These are the drivers Aaron sees on every storm call across Cuyahoga and Geauga counties — none of them wait for business hours.

  • Water intrusion through a breached roofA tree through the roof lets rain destroy ceilings, drywall, and insulation within hours of the next shower.
  • Continued wind drives the tree deeperA partially-failed tree rarely holds. More wind pushes it further into the structure or completes the failure.
  • Energized power lines under the treeLine-adjacent failures are an electrocution and fire hazard until the utility de-energizes. We coordinate — never DIY.
  • Insurance claims denied on delayAdjusters reduce or deny claims when documentation is missing or extraction was delayed. Documenting the scene first protects the claim.

What If You Wait

The Cost of Delaying a Storm-Damaged Tree

Delay compounds storm damage in specific, quantifiable ways — every one drawn from real insurance-claim and emergency-response experience across Cuyahoga and Geauga counties.

Water Intrusion

A breached roof lets rain destroy ceilings, drywall, and insulation within hours of any rainfall — long before the tree itself is removed.

Progressive Structural Damage

Continued wind drives a fallen tree deeper into the structure or completes a partial failure that was, for a few hours, survivable.

Electrocution + Fire Hazard

Energized lines under a downed tree are a life-safety risk until the utility responds. Homeowner attempts to clear them cause serious injuries.

Insurance Claim Complications

Claims grow more complicated the longer the tree remains and the longer extraction is delayed without documentation of the scene.

DIY Fatality Risk

The leading cause of tree-related fatalities in the US is homeowners cutting storm-damaged trees, where spring tension releases violently.

Undetected Hazard Trees

When one tree fails, others nearby often have hidden storm damage. Left unassessed, the next wind event finds them first.

Common Storm & Emergency Questions

Storm Damage & Emergency FAQ

Seven answers before the storm hits. Every one from Aaron's actual emergency-response calls.

What should I do if a tree falls on my house?
First, make sure everyone is safe — stay away from the tree until you've assessed for power lines. If lines are involved, call FirstEnergy / Illuminating Company before approaching. Photograph everything before any cleanup begins. Tarp any roof breach to prevent water intrusion. Call your homeowners insurance claims line within 24 hours to open the claim. Call the Roubic emergency line at {{global.phone}} for tree extraction. Do not attempt DIY removal — storm-damaged trees have unpredictable spring tension and are the leading cause of tree-related fatalities nationally.
Does homeowners insurance cover tree removal after a storm?
Generally yes, when a tree damages a covered structure (house, garage, certain fence types, vehicle in some scenarios). Insurance typically does NOT cover removal of a tree that fell without damaging anything, or routine removal of a healthy tree. Roubic provides documentation — photos, itemized work, species and DBH estimates — built into the storm-response workflow so your claim moves through cleanly.
How quickly can Roubic respond to a storm emergency?
We aim for on-site within 2–4 hours for emergencies inside our primary service area (Auburn Township, Pepper Pike, Chagrin Falls, Moreland Hills, Solon, and the surrounding inner-ring suburbs), and typically 1–2 hours after hours for Tier 1 cities. After-hours and weekend response carries a 50% surcharge over scheduled rates. Tier 2 and Tier 3 markets receive priority but may have slightly longer mobilization times during major regional storm events.
How much does emergency tree service cost?
Emergency, after-hours, and weekend tree service carries a 50% surcharge over scheduled rates. Tree-on-structure removal typically runs $800–$5,000 depending on tree size, structure type, and extraction complexity. Full-property storm cleanup (multi-tree, branches, debris) runs $1,500–$10,000+. Most structural-damage storm work is partially or fully covered by homeowners insurance when a covered structure is damaged.
What if the tree is on a power line?
Call the utility (FirstEnergy / Illuminating Company) FIRST. Assume every downed line is energized until proven otherwise. We will not touch energized lines without utility clearance — that's not stubbornness, it's the life-safety standard for tree services. Once the utility de-energizes the line and clears the scene, we can extract the tree. The wait can be hours during a major regional storm; in the meantime, stay back at least the tree's height from any down line.
Do you work with insurance companies directly?
We don't negotiate the claim on your behalf — that's between you and your adjuster. But we eliminate the documentation friction that causes most claim delays by providing a complete packet (photos, itemized work scope, species and DBH estimates) the morning after the job. Adjusters routinely tell our customers that the Roubic documentation packet is unusually clean compared to typical contractor invoices.
Can I cut up a fallen tree myself if it's just lying in my yard?
If the tree is fully on the ground, not contacting any structure, not contacting any power line, and you have chainsaw experience plus appropriate PPE, sometimes yes — for small trees. Larger trees with spring-loaded limbs, leaning trees, hung trees, or any tree near power lines should always be left to professionals. Storm-damaged trees are the leading cause of tree-related fatalities in the US, and the most common scenario is a homeowner cutting into spring-loaded wood that whips back unexpectedly.
